setup.zh: 出村时，吴婆婆把一块磨亮的木牌塞给你：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」前山满地狗爪印——马家的围猎篦空了它。
setup.en: Leaving the village, Granny Wu pressed a worn token into your hand: "When you reach the stele, look at its back." The front slopes are all dog tracks — the Mas' hunts combed them bare.

recap.zh: 吴婆婆给了你一块狐纹木牌；前山被马家的围猎篦空了。
recap.en: Granny Wu gave you a fox-carved token; the Mas' hunts had combed the front slopes bare.

zh: 村东头，瞎眼的吴婆婆，像在等你们。
一块磨得发亮的小木牌。
前山：满地狗爪印，马蹄印。
en: At the east end, blind Granny Wu, as if she were waiting.
A little wooden token, worn bright.
The front slopes: dog tracks and hoofprints everywhere.

text.zh: 木牌磨得发亮，刻着一只蜷着的狐狸，尾巴一圈圈绕着身子；揣在怀里，温温的。
text.en: The token is rubbed smooth: a curled fox, its tails wound round and round its body. Tucked inside your coat, it is warm.

text.zh: 狗爪印、马蹄印一层叠着一层，连兔子洞都给刨开了——马家篦过的山，连根兔毛都不剩。
text.en: Dog prints and hoofprints lie layer on layer; even the rabbit holes are dug open. Where the Mas have combed a hill, not a rabbit hair is left.

story.zh:
出村要经过村东头。吴婆婆照旧坐在门槛上，一双白蒙蒙的眼睛朝着山的方向，倒像是专门在等他们。吴婆婆是石坳村最老的人，眼睛看不见，耳朵却比村里所有的狗加起来还灵。谁家半夜偷了谁家的瓜，她第二天一早便知道，不但知道是谁偷的，还知道偷了几个，连哪个是生的都知道。

她问道：「去黑松岭？」小满他爹没吭声。吴婆婆也不要他们回答，摸索着从怀里掏出一样东西，塞进小满手里，却是一块小木牌，磨得发亮，上面刻着一只蜷着的狐狸。

吴婆婆道：「你爷爷走的那年，也从我这门口过。」小满张了张嘴，一个字也没说出来。吴婆婆又道：「到了碑那儿，看看碑背面。」小满问：「看什么？」吴婆婆笑了，露出仅剩的三颗牙，道：「看了，就知道了。不看，就不知道。」

小满觉得这句话说了跟没说一样，可还是把木牌揣进了怀里。他娘说过，老人家说话，十句里有九句是废话，剩下那一句，能救命。

那一天，父子两个天没亮就进了山。前山什么也没有，满地都是狗爪印、马蹄印。原来马家入秋办了三场围猎，带着二十条猎狗、几十个家丁，把前山篦了一遍又一遍，篦得比他娘梳头还细。
story.en:
Leaving the village meant passing the east end. Granny Wu sat on her threshold as always, her clouded white eyes turned toward the mountain, as though she'd been waiting just for them. Granny Wu was the oldest person in Shi'ao Village; her eyes couldn't see, but her ears were sharper than every dog in the village put together. If one family stole another's melons in the night she knew by morning — not only who, but how many, and even which ones were unripe.

She asked, "Black Pine Ridge?" Xiaoman's father said nothing. Granny Wu didn't wait for an answer; she fumbled something out of her coat and pressed it into Xiaoman's hand: a little wooden token, rubbed to a shine, carved with a curled-up fox.

Granny Wu said, "The year your grandpa went, he passed this door too." Xiaoman opened his mouth and not a word came out. Granny Wu went on, "When you get to the stele, look at the back of it." Xiaoman asked, "Look at what?" Granny Wu laughed, showing her last three teeth. "Look, and you'll know. Don't look, and you won't."

Xiaoman felt the remark said about as much as nothing, but he tucked the token inside his jacket all the same. His mother had said: of ten things an old person says, nine are nonsense, and the one left over can save your life.

That day father and son went into the mountains before dawn. The front hills held nothing — everywhere dog-paw prints, horse-hoof prints. The Ma family had held three hunts that autumn, with twenty hounds and dozens of servants, and combed the front hills over and over, combed them finer than his mother combed her hair.

label.en: Climb the tallest pine and look out

exits.means: climbs a tree to look out over the mountain, scouts, looks around

story.zh:
小满爬上最高的那棵松树，四下里望了半天，溜下来只说了一句：「爹。前山空了。」

他爹道：「空到什么地步？」小满道：「连耗子都搬家了。门口还贴了告示。」他爹道：「……写的什么？」小满道：「『马家在此，无鼠可活』。」他爹看了他一眼，瞧得出很想笑，但他忍住了，他的膝盖也忍住了。

前山既然空了，他爹便领着他往山里头走。走了一程，他爹忽然站住了，把背上那张弓解下来，拿在手里掂了一掂，道：「今儿教你一样东西。」小满登时来了精神。他爹教他东西，向来是教怎么下套子、怎么认脚印、怎么剥兔子皮，都是手上的活，教完了还要叮嘱一句「别跟你娘说你剥了一下午」。这一回他爹手里拿的却是弓，那便不一样了。那张弓在沈家墙上挂了整整十二年，小满摸过它的弓背，数过弓背上缠了几道牛筋，却从来没有拉过它，他爹不许。

他爹道：「这是你爷爷传下来的，叫《落雁三箭》。」小满道：「落雁？爹，你射下过大雁？」他爹道：「没有。」小满道：「那爷爷射下过？」他爹想了一想，道：「也没有。你爷爷那年去镇上卖皮子，听说书先生讲什么『一箭落雁』，回来便给咱家这点本事起了个名儿。他说，起了名儿，就算武功了。」小满道：「那它到底是不是武功？」他爹道：「是三句话。」小满道：「哪三句？」他爹道：「一箭一句。你爷爷教我，一年只教一箭；我教你，也一年只教一箭。」小满道：「那今年教哪一箭？」他爹道：「头一箭。」说着把弓往地下一拄，一个字一个字地道：「**先看风，后看鹿。**」

小满等了一会儿，见他没有下文，问道：「……完了？」他爹道：「完了。」小满道：「就六个字？」他爹道：「你爷爷教我，也是六个字。」小满心想，一年六个字，照这么教将下去，等他学全了，他爹的膝盖只怕已经聊不动天了。

他爹坐在一块石头上揉着膝盖，许久没有说话，然后站起身来，往山的更深处望了一眼。那边，便是黑松岭。
story.en:
Xiaoman climbed the tallest pine and looked all round for a long time, then slid down and said just one thing: "Dad. The front hills are empty."

His father said, "How empty?" Xiaoman said, "Even the rats have moved house. And put up a notice." His father said, "…Saying what?" Xiaoman said, "'The Mas are here — no rat survives.'" His father looked at him, plainly wanting very much to laugh; but he held it in, and so did his knee.

With the front hills empty, his father led him deeper in. After a stretch his father stopped, unslung the bow and weighed it in his hand. "Today I'll teach you something." Xiaoman perked up at once. When his father taught him things it was always how to set a snare, read a track, skin a rabbit — handwork — and afterwards he'd always add, "Don't tell your mother you spent the afternoon skinning." But this time his father held the bow, and that was different. That bow had hung on the Shens' wall for twelve whole years; Xiaoman had stroked its back and counted its sinew bindings, but never once drawn it. His father didn't allow it.

His father said, "Your grandpa handed this down. It's called *Three Arrows to Fell the Goose*." Xiaoman said, "Fell the goose? Dad, have you ever shot down a goose?" His father said, "No." "Then Grandpa did?" His father thought. "No, not him either. The year your grandpa went to town to sell hides, he heard the storyteller going on about 'one arrow fells the goose', came home, and gave our bit of skill a name. He said once it had a name, it counted as a martial art." "So is it a martial art or not?" "It's three sayings." "Which three?" "One arrow, one saying. Your grandpa taught me one arrow a year; I'll teach you one arrow a year." "Then which arrow this year?" "The first." He planted the bow on the ground and said, word by word: "**First read the wind, then the deer.**"

Xiaoman waited, and when nothing more came, asked, "…That's it?" His father said, "That's it." "Six words?" "Your grandpa taught me six words too." Xiaoman thought: six words a year — at that rate, by the time he'd learned it all, his father's knee would be too old to chat.

His father sat on a rock rubbing his knee and said nothing for a long time; then he stood and looked once, deeper into the mountains. That way lay Black Pine Ridge.
